vocab:Anda / kamu:notes: Anda = formal and distant (ads, documents), kamu = for friends. In conversation people usually say Bapak/Ibu instead
vocab:Bapak / Ibu (Pak / Bu):notes: Polite way to address a man (Pak) or a woman (Bu)
vocab:Mas / Mbak:meaning: bro / sis (friendly title for a young man / woman)
vocab:Mas / Mbak:notes: Use with restaurant and café staff: Mas for men, Mbak for women
vocab:ada:meaning: there is / to have / to be (somewhere)
vocab:akan / bakal:notes: akan = formal future, bakal = casual future (something you expect to happen). mau can do the same job
vocab:bayar:notes: minta bill / mau bayar = Can I get the check?
vocab:belum:notes: A soft way to say no, gentler than a flat "tidak"
vocab:buat / sama / kayak:notes: buat = untuk (for), sama = dengan (with), kayak = seperti (like). In formal settings, use the standard forms
vocab:bukan:notes: Only negates nouns, as in "that's not a…"
vocab:daripada / sama saja:notes: daripada = than (for comparisons), sama saja = it's all the same
vocab:di situ:notes: In between here (di sini) and over there (di sana)
vocab:dia / beliau:notes: dia = he or she, no gender distinction (safe default); beliau = for someone you respect (a boss, an elder)
vocab:dong / sih / kok / nih:notes: They don't mean much on their own, but leave them out and you'll sound foreign. Pick them up by ear
vocab:enak:notes: Works for almost anything: food, mood, how your body feels
vocab:gimana:notes: Casual short form of bagaimana, by far the more common one in everyday speech
vocab:jauh:notes: A must for haggling over a taxi fare: ask "Is it far?"
vocab:kan / iya kan / beneran:notes: kan = right?, iya kan = isn't it?, beneran = for real. A bit of spice for casual conversation
vocab:karena / soalnya:notes: karena is formal / soalnya is casual
vocab:kayaknya / sepertinya:notes: For guessing and softening, when you'd rather not state something outright. This is at the heart of Indonesian culture
vocab:kita / kami:notes: A distinction English doesn't make: kita = includes the listener, kami = excludes the listener
vocab:minta:notes: minta + noun = Can I have ___, please?
vocab:nanti:notes: The go-to polite brush-off: "nanti aja" (maybe later)
vocab:nasi:notes: nasi goreng (fried rice), nasi padang (Padang-style rice with dishes)
vocab:paling / ter-:notes: paling = everyday, ter- = formal prefix (paling enak = terenak)
vocab:pedas:notes: Fair warning: even if you love spicy food, Indonesian spicy is next level
vocab:pengen / kudu:notes: pengen = casual mau, kudu = casual harus. For hanging out and chatting with friends
vocab:permisi:notes: Use it when squeezing past someone or getting someone's attention
vocab:pernah:notes: For experiences. "belum pernah" (I've never done it yet) comes up a lot too
vocab:pulang:meaning: to go home / to go back
vocab:ribu:notes: Indonesian prices are counted in thousands: lima ribu = 5,000 rupiah
vocab:saya / aku:notes: saya = the polite default (safe on business trips), aku = with friends, peers, or a partner. Switch once you get closer
vocab:sebenarnya / sebenernya:notes: For getting to the point or disagreeing. Formal / casual forms
vocab:sebentar / bentar:notes: sebentar = formal, bentar = casual short form
vocab:sedang / lagi:notes: sedang = formal, lagi = casual (much more common). Goes before the verb
vocab:sekali / banget:notes: sekali is formal, banget is casual. Both go after the adjective
vocab:selamat datang:notes: What you'll hear at hotels and restaurants
vocab:selamat pagi / siang / sore / mala: Greetings by time of day: pagi (morning), siang (midday), sore (afternoon), malam (evening)
vocab:suka / tidak suka:notes: Lifesaver: "tidak suka pedas" (I don't like spicy food) is a must at restaurants
vocab:taksi / ojek / Grab / Gojek:notes: Grab and Gojek are Southeast Asian ride-hailing apps
vocab:terima kasih / makasih:notes: makasih is the casual short form
vocab:tidak / nggak / gak:notes: Negates verbs and adjectives. nggak/gak are casual.
